problem: Learning-based (RL) autonomous explorers are mostly restricted to 2D single-floor maps, while classical 3D explorers target aerial robots; multi-floor indoor exploration with ground robots remains open.
motivation: Indoor buildings often have multiple floors connected by stairs, and extending RL observations to full 3D adds excessive complexity. The authors observe that information is dense within a floor but sparse between floors, so a floor-stair topology suffices and lets any 2D explorer be reused.
key_idea: Decompose a multi-floor building into a floor-stair topological graph managed by a finite state machine, and plug an attention-based (ViT) PPO 2D global-goal exploration policy with frontier-guided reward into each floor.
insight: The ablation shows removing attention drops SR from 0.473 to 0.380 (to ANS-level), removing frontier reward drops SR to 0.373 and APL to 1.007, and removing orientation drops SR to 0.410, so all three contribute. The topology decouples floors, so all 2D explorers (Nearest, Utility, RH-NBV, ANS, LITE-2D) work in multi-floor, and the best 2D policy remains best there (1708 steps vs 1777 for ANS).
method: Map representation: 2-channel obstacle/explored grid (M=480, 0.05 m) from depth point clouds plus a 1-channel stair semantic map projected from YOLO11 masks.
Stair detector: YOLO11n-seg fine-tuned on 1,511 web-collected stair images annotated semi-automatically with Labelme+SAM (mAP50-95 0.954).

Attention-based 2D policy: 8xLxL stacked local/global map -> CNN -> P^2=225 patch tokens with learned positional embedding -> transformer encoder -> FC goal head (normal distribution for (x,y)) plus value branch, with orientation embedding; trained with PPO.
Frontier-guided reward: r = area gain + lambda * r_f, where r_f rewards global goals close to frontier edges (piecewise 0 / 0.05/D / 0.005 by distance thresholds).
Floor-stair topology builder: nodes are floor grid maps, edges are detected stairs, incrementally added as new floors/stairs are found.

FSM + policy switcher: states ExploringFloor / GoingToStair / OnStair / AllExplored; the 2D policy is used when exploring, the nearest stair centroid when going to a stair, and an extension of the stair centerline away from the entrance when on the stairs; the local planner is Fast Marching.

setting.backbone: ViT-style attention policy (CNN + transformer encoder, PPO) + YOLO11n-seg stair detector
setting.training_data: Policy: PPO in Habitat on 57 single-floor HM3D training scenes, >15M frames; stair detector: 1,511 self-annotated internet stair images
setting.observation: RGB-D 480x640 (policy takes only the 2D occupancy/explored map plus pose history; RGB used for stair segmentation)
setting.action_space: global goal (x,y) in the local map, executed by a Fast Marching local planner
setting.privileged: none (in simulation, 95% explored ratio used as the floor-done criterion/success)

numbers_note: Tables are complete. Exploration metrics (CR, CA, APL) are not standard navigation benchmarks, so they are listed under 'other'.
results: LITE-2D beats ANS Global on HM3D (CR 0.918 vs 0.901, SR 0.473 vs 0.407) and on MP3D generalization (CR 0.765 vs 0.748, SR 0.323 vs 0.301). In multi-floor HM3D scenes LITE reaches CR 0.929 in 1708 steps versus ANS 0.924 in 1777 and RH-NBV 0.905 in 1736. The system is also shown on a Unitree Aliengo quadruped in a real two-floor building.
limitations: Only a simple floor-stair topology is handled (stairs only, no elevators or complex connectivity); the multi-floor evaluation covers just 6 HM3D scenes with aggregate numbers and no scene-level statistics.
Success rate is low because of reconstruction errors and the step limit; gains over ANS are modest, and there are no multiple seeds or significance tests.
Depends on a stair detector trained on a small web dataset and on rule-based stair traversal; the real-world demo is qualitative only.
